analogy.p: Aerobic respiration is like burning a log fully in plenty of air: you get lots of heat and only ash and gases left. Anaerobic respiration is like a log smouldering with too little air: it releases some heat but leaves charcoal that still holds energy, just like lactic acid or ethanol still contain energy. It breaks down because living cells carry out controlled enzyme reactions, not flames, and lactic acid can be reused by the liver, unlike charcoal in a fire.

bullets: 'An-aerobic' literally means 'without air (oxygen)'.
Like all respiration it is controlled by **enzymes** and occurs in cells.
It does **not** use oxygen, so oxygen does not appear in the equation.
It is a way of keeping energy transfer going when oxygen is limited, but only for a short time in animals.
It happens in the **cytoplasm** of the cell (not the mitochondria).
It is still **exothermic**: heat is released, just less than aerobic.
core.p: **Anaerobic respiration** is respiration that happens **without oxygen**. It still transfers energy from **glucose**, so it is still an **exothermic reaction**, but it is a much less efficient process. It takes place when the oxygen supply is too low for aerobic respiration to keep up, for example in **muscles during vigorous exercise**, or in organisms such as **yeast** that live where oxygen is absent.

bullets: Incomplete breakdown means **less energy** per glucose molecule transferred.
Lactic acid and ethanol still hold energy in their chemical bonds.
This is why anaerobic respiration is a short-term fix in animals: cells need much more glucose to get the same amount of energy.
Aerobic respiration: glucose is broken down **completely** to carbon dioxide and water.
Mark scheme wording: 'glucose is not fully oxidised/broken down'.
Do not say anaerobic 'makes no energy': it makes **some**, just less.
core.h: Why it transfers much less energy
core.p: In anaerobic respiration the glucose is **only partially oxidised** (broken down). The carbon-containing products (lactic acid, or ethanol) still contain a lot of chemical energy that has **not** been released. In aerobic respiration glucose is **completely oxidised** to carbon dioxide and water, which are low-energy molecules, so far more energy is transferred.

bullets: Word equation: **glucose → lactic acid** (plus a small amount of energy transferred).
No carbon dioxide is made, and oxygen is not needed.
The lactic acid builds up in the muscle and blood.
The build-up causes **muscle fatigue**: muscles stop contracting efficiently.
It allows an animal to escape danger or sprint for short bursts even with low oxygen.
Both processes may happen at once: aerobic continues but cannot keep up, so anaerobic provides extra.
core.p: In **animal (muscle) cells** the word equation is **glucose → lactic acid**. During vigorous exercise the muscles need energy faster than the blood can deliver oxygen. The cells therefore supplement aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration to keep contracting. There is **no carbon dioxide** produced, which is an important difference from yeast and plants.

bullets: Word equation: **glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide**.
Ethanol is an alcohol; carbon dioxide is a gas. (Unlike muscles, this one **does** make carbon dioxide.)
Fermentation = anaerobic respiration in yeast (a single-celled fungus).
Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so root cells may switch to anaerobic respiration.
Symbol equation (not required by AQA GCSE, but correct): C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2.
Yeast is used because it grows quickly and its fermentation is reliable.
core.h: Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast: fermentation
core.p: In **plant and yeast cells** the word equation is **glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide**. This type of anaerobic respiration is called **fermentation**. It is **economically important** because it is used to make **bread** and **alcoholic drinks**. Plants can respire this way, for example in waterlogged roots where soil has little oxygen.

bullets: The **carbon dioxide** is the useful product in bread making.
Dough is left in a **warm place** to speed up enzyme action (the best temperature is roughly 30 to 40 degrees C, not too hot).
Baking **kills the yeast** and the ethanol evaporates.
If the dough is too hot (above the optimum) the yeast enzymes denature and it will not rise.
Bread dough is kneaded to develop gluten, which traps the gas bubbles.
Link to enzymes: temperature rises increase the rate until denaturing.
core.p: In bread-making, yeast is mixed with flour, water and sugar. The yeast respires anaerobically in the dough (once the oxygen is used) and produces **carbon dioxide**. The gas forms **bubbles** that make the dough **rise**. When baked, the alcohol evaporates, the gas expands, and the heat kills the yeast, leaving a light, airy texture.

bullets: Yeast ferments sugars in grape juice or barley extract.
Conditions are kept **anaerobic** by sealing the vessel with an airlock so CO2 can escape but air cannot enter.
The ethanol concentration is limited because high concentrations are toxic to yeast.
Distillation can be used to make a higher concentration (spirits).
Economic importance: employment, food and drink industries.
Sugar + yeast in a warm, sealed flask is a common school investigation.
core.p: In alcoholic drinks the useful product is **ethanol**. Yeast ferments sugars from grapes (wine) or from malted barley (beer) in a closed container with no oxygen. The carbon dioxide escapes (or gives fizz). Fermentation stops when the ethanol concentration gets high enough to **kill the yeast** or when the sugar runs out.

bullets: Independent variable examples: temperature, glucose concentration.
Dependent variable: volume of gas per minute or bubbles per minute.
Control variables: mass/volume of yeast, volume of solution, time, flask size.
Boil and cool the water to remove dissolved oxygen, then add a layer of oil.
Rate = volume of gas / time (cm3 per min).
Risk: use eye protection; take care with hot water; wash hands after handling yeast.
core.p: A simple investigation uses a flask of yeast and glucose solution connected by a delivery tube to **limewater**. If the limewater turns **cloudy**, carbon dioxide is being produced. To measure the **rate** you can count bubbles per minute or collect the gas in an upturned measuring cylinder or gas syringe. A layer of oil on top of the solution keeps oxygen out so it is truly anaerobic.

bullets: Lactic acid is **not** a permanent waste: the liver converts it to glucose.
The **oxygen debt** is the extra oxygen needed to react with lactic acid and break it down to carbon dioxide and water.
This is why you keep **breathing heavily** and your heart rate stays high after you stop exercising.
Fitter people can delay anaerobic respiration because their heart and lungs supply oxygen more efficiently.
Use the word **fatigue** in answers: it is the term mark schemes expect.
Blood flow removes lactic acid from muscle.
core.h: Muscle fatigue and the lactic acid problem
core.p: During hard exercise the lactic acid in muscles builds up. This is linked to **muscle fatigue**, when the muscles tire and stop contracting efficiently. After the exercise, the lactic acid must be removed. It is carried in the blood to the **liver**, where it is converted back to glucose, and some is broken down with oxygen. This needs extra oxygen after exercise, called the **oxygen debt** (covered in response to exercise).

bullets: **Glucose breakdown**: aerobic complete; anaerobic incomplete.
**Energy**: aerobic much more; anaerobic much less per glucose.
**Products in muscle**: aerobic CO2 + water; anaerobic lactic acid only.
**Products in yeast/plants**: ethanol + CO2.
**Time**: aerobic can continue for long periods; anaerobic is short-term in animals due to lactic acid.
core.p: Examiners love comparison questions. Always compare the same features: oxygen needed, products, energy transferred and where it is used. For energy, say 'more/less' rather than 'a lot'. **Oxygen**: aerobic needs it; anaerobic does not.

bullets: Less energy per glucose, so glucose is consumed faster.
Lactic acid accumulates and causes fatigue.
The liver needs oxygen to deal with the lactic acid.
Sprint events (100 m) rely more on anaerobic; marathon runners rely on aerobic.
Evolutionary advantage: gives a short burst of energy to escape predators.
Some bacteria live permanently anaerobic (e.g. deep in mud).
core.h: Why can't animals rely on anaerobic respiration?
core.p: Anaerobic respiration is not sustainable in animals because it transfers so little energy per glucose and because lactic acid builds up, causing fatigue and lowering the efficiency of the muscles. The cells would also use up their glucose supplies quickly.

bullets: Lactic acid rises during exercise (anaerobic respiration) and falls in recovery.
Peak lactic acid occurs when exercise stops.
Yeast gas production increases with temperature up to an optimum then falls (enzymes denature).
Rate = change in volume / time.
Read graph values carefully and include units.
Compare using the data: 'at 35 degrees C 40 cm3 compared to 10 cm3 at 15 degrees C'.
core.p: You may be given graphs of lactic acid concentration against time, or tables of gas volume produced by yeast at different temperatures. Describe the trend, quote values, and then explain using the correct process. For rate calculations, divide the amount by time and give units.

bullets: Oxygen debt links to lactic acid being oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.
Enzymes in yeast have an optimum temperature; high temperatures denature them.
The circulation carries lactic acid to the liver and oxygen to muscles.
Anaerobic respiration is exothermic, so a fermenting flask warms slightly.
Compare with photosynthesis, which is endothermic.
In extended answers, structure: what happens, why, and the consequence.
core.h: Higher tier and link to other topics
core.p: Higher tier answers should link anaerobic respiration to the circulatory system, exercise and enzymes. You may be asked to evaluate why someone's heart rate and breathing rate remain high after stopping, using oxygen debt, or to explain the effect of temperature on fermentation using enzyme theory. Link also to the economic uses of microorganisms and to energy transfers.

exam: 'State the equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles' (1 mark): glucose → lactic acid. Do not add CO2.
'State the equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast' (1 mark): glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
'Explain why anaerobic respiration transfers less energy' (2 marks): glucose is not completely oxidised/broken down; the lactic acid or ethanol still contains energy.
'Explain why muscles tire during sprinting' (3 marks): not enough oxygen; anaerobic respiration; lactic acid builds up causing fatigue.
'Describe what happens to lactic acid after exercise' (2 marks): carried by blood to the liver; converted back to glucose (or broken down using oxygen).
Bread making questions: yeast respires, carbon dioxide released, bubbles make dough rise; warm for enzymes; baking kills yeast.
Investigation questions: say how you detect the product (limewater cloudy), how you measure rate (bubbles/volume per minute), and control variables.
Rate calculation: rate = volume / time, units cm3 per min; show the working.
Compare questions: give a similarity or difference for each point, use comparative words (more, less).
6 mark answers: link exercise, oxygen shortage, anaerobic respiration, lactic acid, fatigue, oxygen debt, heart rate and breathing recovery.

mistakes.r: It transfers energy, but much less than aerobic, because glucose is not fully broken down.
Muscles: glucose → lactic acid only. Yeast/plants: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
mistakes.w: Muscles produce lactic acid and carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Lactic acid builds up and causes muscle fatigue; it is carried to the liver and converted back to glucose.
mistakes.w: Lactic acid is a waste that stays in the muscle forever.

mistakes.r: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.
It is respiration without oxygen in cells, usually when oxygen supply to muscles cannot keep up.
mistakes.w: Anaerobic respiration is when you stop breathing.

mistakes.r: Dough rises because of the carbon dioxide gas produced by yeast.
mistakes.w: Dough rises because of the alcohol.

mistakes.r: No oxygen is used; that is the definition.
mistakes.w: Oxygen is a reactant of anaerobic respiration.

mistakes.r: It is less efficient: less energy per glucose, though it can be fast.
mistakes.w: Anaerobic respiration is more efficient because it is quicker.

summary: The specification asks you to know that anaerobic respiration is respiration without oxygen, that it transfers much less energy than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partly oxidised, and to recall the word equations: glucose → lactic acid in muscles, and glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide in plant and yeast cells (fermentation). It matters because it explains muscle fatigue in hard exercise and underpins bread and alcohol making.

Respiration using oxygen, transferring much more energy.
The product of anaerobic respiration in muscle cells.
An alcohol produced by yeast and plant cells in anaerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.
When muscles stop contracting efficiently, linked to lactic acid build-up.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to react with lactic acid and break it down.
A single-celled fungus used in bread making and brewing.

worked.ans: (a) lactic acid; (b) ethanol and carbon dioxide.
worked.q: Name the products of anaerobic respiration in (a) human muscle cells and (b) yeast cells. (3 marks)
steps: (a) Muscle cells make only lactic acid from glucose.
(b) Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.

worked.ans: 1.2 cm3/min at 20 degrees C and 3.0 cm3/min at 35 degrees C; the rate is faster at 35 degrees C because enzymes work faster nearer the optimum temperature.
worked.q: A student measures the volume of carbon dioxide produced by yeast in 15 minutes: 20 degrees C, 18 cm3; 35 degrees C, 45 cm3. Calculate the rate at each temperature and explain the difference. (4 marks)
steps: Rate at 20 degrees C = 18 / 15 = 1.2 cm3 per min.
Rate at 35 degrees C = 45 / 15 = 3.0 cm3 per min.
Higher temperature gives more kinetic energy, so more enzyme-substrate collisions, so a faster rate of fermentation.

worked.ans: Anaerobic respiration made lactic acid during the sprint. After the race the sprinter must repay the oxygen debt: extra oxygen is needed to react with lactic acid (carried to the liver), so breathing rate stays high.
worked.q: Explain why a sprinter's breathing stays fast after finishing a race. (4 marks)
steps: During the sprint the muscles needed more energy than aerobic respiration could supply.
They respired anaerobically, making lactic acid.
After the race, extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid, which is the oxygen debt.
So breathing and heart rate stay high to deliver oxygen and carry lactic acid to the liver.
